newsitem.title: USA: US stocks stage late rally, push Dow to new record.
newsitem.headline: US stocks stage late rally, push Dow to new record.

text.p: A late buying binge on Wall Street helped stocks overcome steep losses on Tuesday and powered the Dow industrials to their second straight record close.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 33 points to close unofficially at 6601, its second straight record close. The Nasdaq Composite also set a new record, rising about 11 points to 1328.

Although gains among blue chips were about the same as those won on Monday, analysts found more reason for optimism in Tuesday's results, which produced a somewhat broader rally and saw the Dow overcome more than 50 points in losses.
"This makes me feel a little bit better about the market," said Gregory Nie, technical analyst at EVEREN Securities. "The comeback this afternoon keeps the door open for the bulls to take control."
Even so, Nie added, the rally was at best a "half-step" forward for stocks, noting, "The rally continues to focus on the upper crust and at some point that becomes troubling."

Analysts were also quick to point to the so-called "January effect," the flood of cash from bonus payments, dividend distributions and annual retirement account contributions that hit mutual funds at the start of the year.
"This is invariably one of the strongest periods for mutual funds," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities.
"There is a natural inclination to put that new money to work, which does explain why January tends to be a successful month for the market," he added.

The new investment also helps explain why stocks have managed a pair of record performances despite continued weakness in the bond market, where the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury fell 7/32, pushing the yield up to 6.79 percent.
Analysts said one worry was sidestepped when Newt Gingrich became the first Republican in 68 years to win a second consecutive term as speaker of the House of Representatives.

"I think it eliminates a cloud over the market because another speaker might not have shown the same dedication to a balanced budget," said Phil Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.

Broad market indicators showed more strength than on Monday. Advancing issues outpaced decliners by about three-to-two on both the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq. NYSE volume was heavy, totalling about 540 million shares.
In individual issues, Santa Fe Pacific Gold Corp rose one point to 15-1/4 after receiving a sweetened takeover offer from Newmont Mining Corp.
Newmont, which boosted its unsolicited offer to 0.4 of a share for each Santa Fe share from 0.33 of a share, fell 3/4 to 40-1/2.
Homestake Mining Co, which has reached a friendly merger deal with Santa Fe, rose 9/16 to 13-11/16. Homestake said it still plans to complete its deal with Santa Fe.

UST Inc fell 2-5/8 to 30-3/4 after warning its fourth quarter sales and earnings would fall short of estimates. The company cited lower than expected sales of its smokeless tobacco products. UST owns Skoal and Copenhagen, which are the two leading brands of smokeless tobacco.
General Instrument Corp rose 1/2 to 23-1/4. The company announced a broad restructuring under which it will split into three publicly-traded companies.

General Instrument said it will spin off its cable, satellite and communications business into one of the companies. A second will focus on coaxial and high performance cable manufacturing and the third will be comprised of its power semiconductor division.
The S&P 500 rose 5.58 to 753.23.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 11.33 to a record 1327.73.
(Figures official as of 1645 EST/2145 GMT).
-- Wall Street desk 212 859 1721
